```{r setup}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(comment = "#>", fig.align = "center")
library(forestsearch)
library(survival)
```

`forestsearch()` searches a trial for a subgroup in which the treatment effect
is worse than the trial's, from candidates built as conjunctions of at most two
covariate cuts, and reports the effect in the identified subgroup and in its
complement with estimates and bounds that account for the selection. This
vignette runs the analysis reported as Table 1 of León and Anderson (2026b), on
the German Breast Cancer Study Group (GBSG) trial that ships with **survival**,
at the manuscript's settings: the three identifiers of that paper — forest
search (FS), the cross-fit surface (DINA) and the causal forest (GRF) — each by
one call, then the selection-adjusted analysis of León and Anderson (2026a) on
each identified region and its complement. The search is described in León and
Anderson (2026b); the corrected estimate, the one-sided field bounds and the
two-subgroup claim in León and Anderson (2026a); the original procedure in León
et al. (2024). The computation takes about a minute and a half on one core;
the fit times are printed as they are measured.

## The data

The analysis set is the 686 patients with complete prognostic data, out of 720
randomized: 246 received hormonal therapy and 440 did not, with 299 recurrences
or deaths. Seven covariates enter the search: age, menopausal status, tumour
size, grade, the number of positive lymph nodes, and the progesterone and
estrogen receptor concentrations in fmol/l. Randomization status is masked in
the distributed data; hormonal therapy is analysed as randomized.

```{r data}
df <- survival::gbsg
df <- within(df, {
  id          <- seq_len(nrow(df))              # the fit's subject identifier
  time_months <- rfstime / 30.4375              # recurrence-free survival, days to months
  grade3      <- ifelse(grade == "3", 1, 0)     # grade 3 against grade 1 or 2
})
confounders <- c("age", "meno", "size", "grade3", "nodes", "pgr", "er")
stopifnot(nrow(df) == 686, sum(df$status) == 299)

whole <- coxph(Surv(time_months, status) ~ hormon, data = df)
whole_hr <- c(est = unname(exp(coef(whole))), exp(confint(whole))[1, ])
c(patients = nrow(df), hormonal_therapy = sum(df$hormon == 1),
  none = sum(df$hormon == 0), events = sum(df$status))
sprintf("Whole-trial hazard ratio %.3f (%.3f, %.3f), hormonal therapy vs none",
        whole_hr[["est"]], whole_hr[[2]], whole_hr[[3]])
```

Every bound below is read against the trial's own effect, a hazard ratio of
`r sprintf("%.3f", whole_hr[["est"]])`, and against clinically meaningful
effect sizes — not as a test at a hazard ratio of one.

## The specification

Candidates are conjunctions of at most two covariate cuts (`maxk = 2`) with
more than 60 patients (`n.min`); forest search additionally requires ten events
in each arm (`d0.min`, `d1.min`). Continuous covariates take the package's
default cuts, except that the two receptors carry ten candidate cuts each
(`conf.cont_jcuts`) with the value zero — no measured receptor — forced in as a
cut of its own (`conf_force`).

Three thresholds govern the search, on the hazard-ratio scale with harm
upward:

- the **screening threshold** c₁ = `hr.threshold`, which a candidate's
  estimated hazard ratio must clear to be admitted;
- the **per-split threshold** c₂ = `hr.consistency`, the claim threshold at
  which an effect stops being beneficial, which both halves of a random
  half-split must clear for the split to count as consistent;
- the **consistency level** p\* = `pconsistency.threshold`, the proportion of
  consistent splits a candidate must reach.

The applications of León and Anderson (2026b) set c₁ = c₂ = 1.0 and
p\* = 0.90. The splitting-consistency rate is *not* computed by drawing splits.
With `consistency_method = "resample"` (the default) the rate is evaluated in
closed form, as Section 2.2 of that paper gives it: to first order the two
half-sample estimates are a mirror pair about the full-sample fit, so the
probability that both clear c₂ is 2Φ((β̂(g) − log c₂)/σ_D(g)) − 1, with σ_D(g)
the scale of the half-sample difference obtained from the fit's influence
function. Despite its name, `"resample"` draws nothing. Literal random
half-splitting (`consistency_method = "split"`, `fs.splits` refits per
candidate) is retained only as the fallback for a candidate whose closed form
cannot be evaluated — a non-convergent fit, for instance — and `fs.splits` has
no effect otherwise. Here every candidate has at least ten events in each arm
and the Cox fits converge, so the closed form is evaluable throughout and the
search is deterministic given the data. The rate is rounded to
`pconsistency.digits = 2` decimals before it is compared with p\*.

The **selection rule** is max N(ε): among the admitted candidates, the largest
whose hazard ratio is within 20% of the largest hazard ratio over the family
(`sg_focus = "effMaxSG"`, `selection_rule = "neighborhood"`,
`effect_neighborhood = 0.20`). Section 2.1 of León and Anderson (2026b) sets
this rule beside the alternatives (max N, max β, and their smallest-subgroup
counterparts), which Figure 1 of that paper draws on this trial's candidate
frontier.

**Inference** (`mr_inference = TRUE`) follows León and Anderson (2026a): from
5,000 multiplier draws over every size-eligible candidate the identifier
proposes, the corrected (two-term) estimate of the effect in the identified
region Ĥ and in its complement Ĥᶜ; the nominal 95% one-sided *field* lower
bound on β(Ĥ); the *field-s* upper bound on β(Ĥᶜ), the studentized complement
bound; and the Bonferroni pair, a joint 95% claim on both. The field's own
Monte Carlo runs at 1,000 outer and 500 inner draws, the package's fixed
setting on this path. The only randomness in the analysis is in these draws;
they are seeded by `seedit`, so the vignette's numbers are reproducible.

## Forest search

One call. Identification, the unadjusted estimates and every selection-adjusted
quantity come out of it together. `parallel_args = list(plan = "sequential")`
keeps the run on one core; the package's default plan is parallel.

```{r fit-fs}
#| message: false
#| results: hide
t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
fit_fs <- forestsearch(
  df.analysis = df,
  outcome.name = "time_months", event.name = "status", treat.name = "hormon", id.name = "id",
  confounders.name = confounders,
  is.RCT = TRUE, est.scale = "hr", seedit = 8316951,
  # the candidate family
  conf.cont_jcuts = list(er = 10, pgr = 10), conf_force = c("er <= 0", "pgr <= 0"),
  n.min = 60, d0.min = 10, d1.min = 10, maxk = 2,
  # the identifier, its thresholds and the selection rule
  subgroup_method = "consistency", consistency_method = "resample",
  hr.threshold = 1.00, hr.consistency = 1.00, pconsistency.threshold = 0.90,
  stop_threshold = NULL,                      # evaluate every candidate; no early stop
  sg_focus = "effMaxSG", selection_rule = "neighborhood", effect_neighborhood = 0.20,
  # selection-adjusted inference
  mr_inference = TRUE,
  mr_inference_args = list(ci_method = "field", draws = 5000L, include_complement = TRUE,
                           field_scale_complement = "selected", field_decompose = TRUE,
                           keep_declaration_field = TRUE,
                           declaration_c0 = c(0.70, 0.75, 0.80, 0.85)),
  quiet = TRUE, parallel_args = list(plan = "sequential"))
fit_sec_fs <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
```

```{r fs-selected}
g_fs <- fit_fs$mr_inference
cat(sprintf("Identified subgroup: %s\n", paste(fit_fs$sg.harm, collapse = " & ")))
cat(sprintf("Fit including inference: %.1f s (multiplier stage %.1f s; field blocks %.1f + %.1f s)\n",
            fit_sec_fs, g_fs$timing_seconds, g_fs$field$timing_seconds,
            g_fs$field$complement$timing_seconds))
```

The identified region is `r sprintf("\x60%s\x60", paste(fit_fs$sg.harm, collapse = " & "))`:
no measured estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor at most 26 fmol/l. Two
arguments in the call are not the defaults and are there for a reason:
`stop_threshold = NULL` has the consistency stage evaluate every screened
candidate rather than stop at the first that passes, and
`field_decompose = TRUE` returns the supporting quantities shown below.
Everything else that is not the default is the specification itself.

### The search in numbers

The fit records how the candidates were whittled down. Supplementary Table S13
of León and Anderson (2026b) reports the same funnel.

```{r fs-funnel}
counts <- fit_fs$find.grps$filter_counts
funnel <- data.frame(
  stage = c("enumerated (at most two cuts, size-eligible)",
            "fittable (ten events in each arm, Cox fit obtained)",
            "clearing the screening threshold, HR > 1.0",
            "passing the consistency screen, p_cons >= 0.90",
            "re-selection family for inference"),
  candidates = c(counts$n_evaluated, counts$n_passed_cox, counts$n_passed_hr,
                 fit_fs$grp.consistency$n_passed, g_fs$n_family))
knitr::kable(funnel, row.names = FALSE, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```

The re-selection family is larger than the screened set: multiplier resampling
re-selects over every size-eligible candidate under the screening threshold and
the consistency screen, without the per-arm event minimum, so the family
contains the one the search ranked (Supplementary Section S5).

The candidates that pass the screen, with their size, hazard ratio and
consistency rate, are the points of Figure 1 of the paper. The selection rule
acts on them.

```{r fs-candidates}
cand <- as.data.frame(fit_fs$grp.consistency$out_sg$result)
cand$candidate <- ifelse(cand$M.2 == "", cand$M.1, paste(cand$M.1, cand$M.2, sep = " & "))
cand <- cand[order(-cand$N), ]
knitr::kable(cand[, c("candidate", "N", "hr", "Pcons")], digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("candidate", "N", "HR", "p_cons"),
             caption = "The candidates passing the consistency screen, largest first.")
band <- (1 - 0.20) * max(cand$hr)
within_band <- cand$hr >= band
sel <- cand[within_band, ][which.max(cand$N[within_band]), ]
cat(sprintf("Largest HR over the family: %.2f (N %d). Band: HR >= %.2f.\n",
            max(cand$hr), cand$N[which.max(cand$hr)], band))
cat(sprintf("max N(eps) takes the largest candidate within the band: N %d, HR %.2f.\n", sel$N, sel$hr))
cat(sprintf("max N alone would take N %d (HR %.2f); max beta the N %d.\n",
            max(cand$N), cand$hr[which.max(cand$N)], cand$N[which.max(cand$hr)]))
stopifnot(sel$N == g_fs$n_selected)      # the rule, re-applied here, picks the fit's own selection
```

All of the passing candidates restrict the estrogen receptor, and the rules
differ only in how far that region is trimmed. The max N(ε) rule takes the 75
patients with no measured estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor at most
26 fmol/l; max N would take the 82 with no measured estrogen receptor; the
effect-maximising rules the 61 with, in addition, tumour size at most 35 mm.

## The selection-adjusted analysis of a region

The nine quantities of Table 1 are read from `fit$mr_inference`. There is no
single accessor for them, so the vignette defines one; `print(fit)` and
`summary(fit)` report the bounds and the diagnostics in their own layout.

```{r table1-helper}
table1_column <- function(fit, data) {
  g  <- fit$mr_inference; cc <- g$complement; fb <- g$field; fc <- fb$complement; js <- fb$joint_s
  in_H <- fit$df.est$treat.recommend[match(data$id, fit$df.est$id)] == 0
  stopifnot(!anyNA(in_H), sum(in_H) == g$n_selected, sum(!in_H) == cc$n)
  f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
  ci <- function(e, l, u) sprintf("%s (%s, %s)", f3(e), f3(l), f3(u))
  c(paste(fit$sg.harm, collapse = " & "),
    sprintf("%d (%d)", sum(in_H), sum(data$status[in_H])),
    ci(g$naive$est, g$naive$lower, g$naive$upper),
    f3(g$debiased$est),
    f3(fb$lower_1s),
    sprintf("%d (%d)", sum(!in_H), sum(data$status[!in_H])),
    ci(cc$naive$est, cc$naive$lower, cc$naive$upper),
    f3(cc$debiased$est),
    f3(fc$upper_1s_s),
    sprintf("%s / %s", f3(js$bonf_lower_H), f3(js$bonf_upper_Hc)))
}
table1_rows <- c("Region", "N (events)", "Unadjusted, 95% CI", "Corrected", "Field, lower bound",
                 "Complement N (events)", "Unadjusted, 95% CI", "Corrected", "Field-s, upper bound",
                 "Bonferroni pair")
knitr::kable(data.frame(row = table1_rows, FS = table1_column(fit_fs, df)),
             col.names = c("", "FS"), row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Forest search: the identified region and its complement, hazard-ratio scale.")
```

The unadjusted hazard ratio in the region is opposite in direction to the
trial's; the correction removes
`r sprintf("%.3f", g_fs$selection_bias)` on the log scale and leaves
`r sprintf("%.3f", g_fs$debiased$est)`. The field lower bound is the one-sided
95% bound on the region's effect; the field-s upper bound the one-sided 95%
bound on the complement's; the Bonferroni pair is both at joint 95%, each side
at 0.975.

The quantities that support the bounds, as in Supplementary Table S18 of the
paper:

```{r fs-supporting}
fb <- g_fs$field; fc <- fb$complement; js <- fb$joint_s
supporting <- data.frame(
  quantity = c("mean of the simulated selection root, region (log scale)",
               "second-order estimate, region",
               "second-order estimate, complement (field-s)",
               "scale ratio rho_c (field-s vs the unstudentized complement bound)",
               "Bonferroni pair: simulated joint coverage",
               "calibrated split gamma (Bonferroni's own alpha/2 is 0.025)",
               "correlation of the aligned roots"),
  value = c(sprintf("%.3f", fb$lambda_mean), sprintf("%.3f", fb$est2), sprintf("%.3f", fc$est2_s),
            sprintf("%.3f", fc$decomp_fields$scale_ratio_c), sprintf("%.4f", js$bonf_joint_prob),
            sprintf("%.3f", js$gamma), sprintf("%.3f", js$corr)))
knitr::kable(supporting, row.names = FALSE)
```

The second-order estimate subtracts from the corrected estimate the mean of the
simulated selection root; the bound subtracts a quantile of the same law and is
not centred on it. A scale ratio near one means field-s and the unstudentized
complement bound agree on these data.

## The two model-based identifiers

DINA and GRF propose candidates from a surface fitted to the outcome and have
them re-ranked on the same Cox coefficient β̂(g) against the same screening
threshold; neither applies the consistency screen. Supplementary Section S5 of
León and Anderson (2026b) sets the three identifiers side by side, with every
setting used here. The selection rule and the inference are the same. The
calls differ from forest search's only in the identifier's own arguments.

```{r fit-dina}
#| message: false
#| results: hide
t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
fit_dina <- forestsearch(
  df.analysis = df,
  outcome.name = "time_months", event.name = "status", treat.name = "hormon", id.name = "id",
  confounders.name = confounders,
  is.RCT = TRUE, est.scale = "hr", seedit = 8316951,
  conf.cont_jcuts = list(er = 10, pgr = 10), conf_force = c("er <= 0", "pgr <= 0"),
  n.min = 60, d0.min = 10, d1.min = 10, maxk = 2,
  subgroup_method = "dina", dina_select_statistic = "effect",     # DINA's own
  hr.threshold = 1.00, stop_threshold = NULL,
  sg_focus = "effMaxSG", selection_rule = "neighborhood", effect_neighborhood = 0.20,
  mr_inference = TRUE,
  mr_inference_args = list(ci_method = "field", draws = 5000L, include_complement = TRUE,
                           field_scale_complement = "selected", field_decompose = TRUE),
  quiet = TRUE, parallel_args = list(plan = "sequential"))
fit_sec_dina <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
```

```{r fit-grf}
#| message: false
#| results: hide
t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
fit_grf <- forestsearch(
  df.analysis = df,
  outcome.name = "time_months", event.name = "status", treat.name = "hormon", id.name = "id",
  confounders.name = confounders,
  is.RCT = TRUE, est.scale = "hr", seedit = 8316951,
  conf.cont_jcuts = list(er = 10, pgr = 10), conf_force = c("er <= 0", "pgr <= 0"),
  n.min = 60, d0.min = 10, d1.min = 10, maxk = 2,
  subgroup_method = "grf", grf_selection = "frontier",             # GRF's own
  grf_select_statistic = "effect", grf_depth = 2L, dmin.grf = 0.0, # GRF's own
  hr.threshold = 1.00, stop_threshold = NULL,
  sg_focus = "effMaxSG", selection_rule = "neighborhood", effect_neighborhood = 0.20,
  mr_inference = TRUE,
  mr_inference_args = list(ci_method = "field", draws = 5000L, include_complement = TRUE,
                           field_scale_complement = "selected", field_decompose = TRUE),
  quiet = TRUE, parallel_args = list(plan = "sequential"))
fit_sec_grf <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
```

```{r dina-grf-selected}
g_dina <- fit_dina$mr_inference
g_grf  <- fit_grf$mr_inference
cat(sprintf("DINA: %s  (fit %.1f s; re-selection family %d)\n",
            paste(fit_dina$sg.harm, collapse = " & "), fit_sec_dina, g_dina$n_family))
cat(sprintf("GRF:  %s  (fit %.1f s; re-selection family %d)\n",
            paste(fit_grf$sg.harm, collapse = " & "), fit_sec_grf, g_grf$n_family))
```

GRF returns the `r g_grf$n_selected` patients with no measured estrogen
receptor, a region that contains forest search's; DINA returns the
`r g_dina$n_selected` who are grade 3 with progesterone receptor at most
20 fmol/l, a different classification. For the two model-based identifiers the
candidate family is generated from a surface fitted to the outcome, so their
bounds are conditional on the family proposed (Supplementary Section S1.9 of
León and Anderson 2026b); forest search's family is enumerated from the
covariates alone.

```{r agreement}
member <- function(fit) fit$df.est$treat.recommend[match(df$id, fit$df.est$id)] == 0
m <- data.frame(FS = member(fit_fs), DINA = member(fit_dina), GRF = member(fit_grf))
partition <- aggregate(cbind(N = 1, events = df$status), by = m, FUN = sum)
knitr::kable(partition[order(-partition$N), ], row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "The three-way partition of the 686 patients by the three selections.")
```

## Table 1

```{r table1}
table1 <- data.frame(row = table1_rows, FS = table1_column(fit_fs, df),
                     DINA = table1_column(fit_dina, df), GRF = table1_column(fit_grf, df))
knitr::kable(table1, col.names = c("", "FS", "DINA", "GRF"), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrr",
             caption = sprintf(paste(
               "Selection-adjusted analysis of the three identified regions, hazard-ratio scale.",
               "Unadjusted: two-sided 95%% Wald interval; field and field-s: one-sided at nominal 0.95;",
               "Bonferroni pair: region / complement, joint 0.95. Whole trial: %d patients, %d events,",
               "hazard ratio %.3f (%.3f, %.3f)."),
               nrow(df), sum(df$status), whole_hr[["est"]], whole_hr[[2]], whole_hr[[3]]))
```

This is Table 1 of León and Anderson (2026b). The calls, the seed and the draw
counts are those of the manuscript's analysis, so the published values are
reproduced to the digit; a different draw count would move the corrected
estimates and the bounds in the third decimal and leave the regions and the
unadjusted estimates unchanged.

### Reading the table

Each estimate is read by its location against the trial's own effect,
`r sprintf("%.3f", whole_hr[["est"]])`; the bounds are reported beside it and
are not read as tests at a hazard ratio of one. A corrected estimate above 0.90
is read as suggestive of limited benefit, and where its lower bound lies below
1.0 a benefit cannot be ruled out.

```{r reading-values}
#| echo: false
r3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
ev_region <- vapply(m, function(z) sum(df$status[z]), numeric(1))
```

- **Forest search.** The unadjusted hazard ratio in its region is
  `r r3(g_fs$naive$est)`, opposite in direction to the trial's. The correction
  leaves `r r3(g_fs$debiased$est)`, above 0.90, so suggestive of limited
  benefit; with a field lower bound of `r r3(g_fs$field$lower_1s)`, below 1.0,
  a benefit cannot be ruled out. The complement,
  `r round(100 * g_fs$complement$n / nrow(df))`% of the trial, has a corrected
  estimate of `r r3(g_fs$complement$debiased$est)`, a larger benefit than the
  trial's, with a field-s upper bound of
  `r r3(g_fs$field$complement$upper_1s_s)`.
- **DINA and GRF** read the same way: corrected estimates of
  `r r3(g_dina$debiased$est)` and `r r3(g_grf$debiased$est)` in their regions,
  with lower bounds below 1.0, and of `r r3(g_dina$complement$debiased$est)`
  and `r r3(g_grf$complement$debiased$est)` in their complements.
- **The two-subgroup claim.** Forest search's Bonferroni pair is
  `r r3(g_fs$field$joint_s$bonf_lower_H)` for the region and
  `r r3(g_fs$field$joint_s$bonf_upper_Hc)` for the complement. The complement's
  benefit, a hazard reduction of at least
  `r round(100 * (1 - g_fs$field$joint_s$bonf_upper_Hc))`%, survives the joint
  adjustment; the region excludes only hazard ratios below
  `r r3(g_fs$field$joint_s$bonf_lower_H)`, which is no claim of harm. A claim
  that the two subgroups differ is not supported; the claim of benefit outside
  the region is.
- **The substantive reading** is the same under all three partitions: a small
  region whose unfavourable unadjusted estimate the correction largely removes,
  and a complement, most of the trial, with a corrected benefit larger than the
  trial's. With `r min(ev_region)` to `r max(ev_region)` events in the regions,
  a claim of harm at a conventional level is not realistic at this trial's
  size; the bounds are reported, and how much statistical assurance to require
  of them is the analyst's decision in their own setting.

## Declaration at a protected level

Every region above was declared at the identifiers' default settings, forest
search's by the conventional screen at p\* = 0.90. Section 4 of León and
Anderson (2026b) asks a different question: would a screen calibrated to
protect a clinically meaningful uniform benefit have declared it? The answer is
read for forest search, whose family is enumerated. At a protected level c₀ and
family-wise level α, the calibrated cutoff κ̂_α(c₀) is the (1 − α) quantile of
the maximum over the family of each candidate's standardized statistic
T(g) = (β̂(g) − log c₂)/σ_D(g), with every candidate shifted to sit at c₀,
under the law of the fit's own multiplier draws. The calibrated rule admits a
candidate when T(g) ≥ κ̂; it holds the family-wise probability of declaring any
harm subgroup at α whenever every candidate's true effect is c₀ or better.
`fs_declaration_calibration()` reads it from the draws the fit above already
made (`keep_declaration_field = TRUE`, with the grid passed as
`declaration_c0`); nothing is redrawn and nothing else in the fit changes.

```{r declaration}
c0_grid <- c(0.70, 0.75, 0.80, 0.85)
cal    <- fs_declaration_calibration(fit_fs, alpha = 0.10, c0 = c0_grid)
cal_c2 <- fs_declaration_calibration(fit_fs, alpha = 0.10)          # c0 = NULL: the claim threshold itself
tb <- cal$c0$table
fld <- g_fs$declaration_field
T_H   <- cal$T_hat[[fld$family_id[fld$meta$selected_index]]]
T_max <- max(cal$T_hat)
kappa <- c(tb$kappa_hat, cal_c2$kappa_hat)
declaration <- data.frame(
  c0 = c(sprintf("HR %.2f%s", tb$c0, ifelse(tb$c0 == 0.75, " (primary)", "")),
         "HR 1.00, the claim threshold"),
  kappa   = sprintf("%.3f", kappa),
  implied = sprintf("%.3f", 2 * pnorm(kappa) - 1),
  fw      = sprintf("%.3f", c(tb$fw_size, cal_c2$fw_size)),
  admits  = c(lengths(cal$c0$admitted_calibrated), length(cal_c2$admitted_calibrated)))
knitr::kable(declaration, row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrr",
             col.names = c("protected level c0", "calibrated cutoff kappa-hat (alpha 0.10)",
                           "implied screening level 2*Phi(kappa-hat) - 1",
                           "family-wise size of the p* = 0.90 screen at c0",
                           "candidates the calibrated rule admits"))
cat(sprintf("T of the declared region: %.3f; largest T in the family: %.3f; the p* = 0.90 screen's cutoff: %.3f\n",
            T_H, T_max, cal$z_pstar))
```

The screen's cutoff is the p\* = 0.90 rule as the package applies it, after
the rate is rounded to `pconsistency.digits = 2`, which is why it sits a little
below the 1.645 of an unrounded 0.90.

At the primary protected level, a hazard ratio of 0.75, the calibrated cutoff
is `r sprintf("%.3f", tb$kappa_hat[tb$c0 == 0.75])`, an implied screening
level of `r sprintf("%.3f", 2 * pnorm(tb$kappa_hat[tb$c0 == 0.75]) - 1)`; the
region's statistic is `r sprintf("%.3f", T_H)` and the largest in the family
`r sprintf("%.3f", T_max)`, so the calibrated screen admits
`r if (lengths(cal$c0$admitted_calibrated)[tb$c0 == 0.75] == 0) "no candidate" else "a candidate"`
at that level, and likewise at every protected level on the grid and at the
claim threshold. The family-wise size in the fourth column is the diagnostic of
the paper's equation (8): the probability that the p\* = 0.90 screen as
executed declares some harm subgroup if every candidate carried a uniform
benefit of c₀ — a property of this family and covariate design, not the
trial's realized error rate; at the claim threshold it is a boundary size.
To run the screen at the implied level, set `pconsistency.threshold` to it and
`pconsistency.digits` to at least 5, so the level is not rounded away; the
package's `pstar_settable` and `pstar_fine` columns in `cal$c0$table` give what
the digit grid can express. The supplement's Section S1.8.4 adds a
realized-rate simulation on this design, which is not run here. The selection
and every bound above are those of the fit as run; the calibration reads the
fit and alters none of them.

## Where to go next

- `vignette("survival-post-selection")` reads the bounds in more depth on the
  same trial: the re-selection frequency p̂ as a diagnostic, membership
  agreement, and what each construction does and does not say.
- The package website carries the original workflow of León et al. (2024) —
  the full argument listing, the bootstrap bias correction and the
  cross-validation — as the article *Exploratory subgroup identification with
  forestsearch (the 2024 workflow)*, and the methodology and simulation
  articles.
- `?forestsearch` documents every argument, with examples for this analysis and
  for the binary and continuous ACTG 175 analyses of León and Anderson
  (2026b), and a section on the options not tested against the manuscript
  analyses.
